items.title: The gh command
items.text: Use a scoped token, validate request inputs and event payloads, check HTTP/error status, handle pagination and rate limits, and avoid logging credentials or unneeded private response data.

items.title: Authentication in workflows
items.text: Make the workflow contract explicit: identify the event, job runner, inputs, command/action, output, and failure signal. Keep steps small and review the permissions and source of every action.

items.title: Creating issues and pull requests
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Working with structured command output
items.text: Write one step output as `name=value` to `$GITHUB_OUTPUT`, then declare job outputs if a downstream job needs the value. Use `$GITHUB_ENV` for values needed by later steps in the same job.

# Example: read a repository field through GitHub CLI
gh api repos/$GITHUB_REPOSITORY --jq '.full_name'
content_blocks.expected_output: With the CLI authenticated and the token permitted, the command prints the repository full name as a single value.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Run inside a workflow with `GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}` in the step environment and the narrowest required `permissions`. Never print the token.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to using github cli in workflows. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain using github cli in workflows, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Use GitHub APIs and CLI integration with explicit authentication, bounded permissions, and handled failures.

content.task: Apply using github cli in workflows to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: GitHub CLI (`gh`) can automate issues, pull requests, runs, and releases when authenticated with a scoped workflow token.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: GitHub CLI (`gh`) can automate issues, pull requests, runs, and releases when authenticated with a scoped workflow token. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: GitHub CLI (`gh`) can automate issues, pull requests, runs, and releases when authenticated with a scoped workflow token.
External integrations need explicit authentication, narrow permissions, input validation, rate-limit handling, deduplication, and safe reporting that does not leak credentials or payloads.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
